overview: This bill would create the Truth and Healing Commission on Indian Boarding School Policies, a temporary body within the legislative branch. For more than a century, federal policy sent many Native American children to boarding schools designed to strip away their languages, cultures and religions, where many suffered abuse. The commission, made up of five members chosen by congressional leaders from nominees put forward by tribes and Native organizations, would investigate these policies and their lasting effects, gather records from federal agencies and religious institutions that ran schools, and hold trauma-informed hearings where survivors can testify. It would issue public reports and recommend how the federal government can acknowledge its role and support healing. The bill also clarifies that federal repatriation law applies to remains and cultural items from these schools and allows reburial on federal land, and the commission would end six years after the law takes effect. As of July 31, 2025, the Senate Indian Affairs Committee had approved it and it was placed on the Senate calendar.
for: Supporters say a full, official accounting of the boarding school era is needed to give survivors and their families a voice, recover records and remains, and help Native communities heal.
against: Critics say the Interior Department has already investigated this history, and a new six-year commission could duplicate that work and add cost, while religious institutions may object to requests for their records.
